argument_summary: Certification is supportable only in a narrow sense: admissible evidence supports operational launch readiness through aggregate pass margin, no severity-one rehearsal incidents, and a 6% reversible rollout with monitoring. The same admissible record does not fully satisfy the disclosure-policy predicate because the affected small-business onboarding use case remains exposed, the segment is below target, and the available risk-acceptance draft is unsigned and incomplete. The strongest defensible packet is therefore certification with an explicit caveat that policy support is weaker than operational readiness support.
claims_about_business_cost: The admissible record supports that the release posture is bounded operationally because rollout begins at 6% and includes rollback and monitoring. That limits downside if issues appear, but business cost or launch velocity should not be treated as a substitute for the unresolved policy condition.
claims_about_policy: The admissible evidence supports distinguishing operational readiness from disclosure compliance. Aggregate readiness, absence of severity-one incidents, rollout controls, and monitoring support readiness to launch in a controlled and reversible posture. But the policy text and admissible policy note indicate those controls do not by themselves cure a material model-card weakness when the affected named use case remains exposed. On the present record, full policy compliance is not established through rollout controls alone; the defensible position is a caveated certification framing rather than an unconditional compliance claim.
concessions: The small-business onboarding segment remains exposed in the initial rollout cohort.
That segment is below target on long-context onboarding support.
The current risk-acceptance draft is unsigned and does not mention the exposed small-business onboarding segment.
The certification case is materially stronger on aggregate readiness than on the disclosure-policy requirement.
